topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
scope_note: Everyday peer and manager feedback at work: why vague feedback fails, the situation-behaviour-impact structure plus a concrete next step, timing and dialogue, specific positive feedback, and the sandwich method. Not disciplinary or HR process, not a tour of models, not receiving feedback.

facts.statement: General feedback, whether praise or criticism, tends not to change behaviour because it does not tell the person which specific action to repeat or to do differently.
facts.caveat: This is a well-supported practical reasoning, not a single measured effect. Say 'tends not to', not 'never'. A pleasant talk is not evidence that anything changed; the test is what the person does next time.
facts.reference_hint: Hattie and Timperley (2007), The Power of Feedback, Review of Educational Research

facts.statement: Feedback does not reliably improve performance: a large meta-analysis of feedback interventions found that on average it helped somewhat, but the effect varied widely and in a substantial share of cases performance got worse.
facts.caveat: Kluger and DeNisi (1996) combined many studies, mostly not from everyday office settings. Use it only as a direction: how feedback is given matters, and good intentions are not enough. Do not quote percentages.
facts.reference_hint: Kluger and DeNisi (1996), Psychological Bulletin, meta-analysis of feedback interventions

facts.statement: Feedback that pulls attention to the person or the self, rather than to the task or the action, is the kind most linked to weak or negative effects on performance.
facts.caveat: Comes from feedback intervention theory (Kluger and DeNisi 1996) and is echoed in Hattie and Timperley (2007), where praise about the person carries little information about the task. Evidence is largely from lab and education settings; state it as a direction, not a guarantee.
facts.reference_hint: Kluger and DeNisi (1996); Hattie and Timperley (2007)

facts.statement: Useful feedback describes what the person did, meaning what could be seen or heard in a specific situation, rather than a label for their character or a guess about their intent.
facts.caveat: Widely taught practice; the strongest support is the reasoning that behaviour can be observed and changed, while intent and character cannot be seen and invite defence. Not shown to work every time.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, Situation-Behavior-Impact guidance

facts.statement: The Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) model from the Center for Creative Leadership structures feedback as the situation, the observed behaviour, and the impact it had.
facts.caveat: It is a well-known, widely used practitioner framework with a named source. It has not been shown by head-to-head trials to beat other structures, so present it as a useful, established structure, not as proven best. Name it at most once, and only as one structure.

facts.statement: Stating the impact means saying what the behaviour did to the work, the people or the results, which explains why it matters to the person hearing it.
facts.caveat: Practice guidance from the SBI approach; keep the impact factual and about the work or others, not about the giver's mood alone.

facts.statement: Effective feedback also points forward: it says or agrees what to do next, which answers the question 'where to next' for the person.
facts.caveat: SBI itself stops at impact; the concrete next step is a common practitioner addition, supported by the feedback literature that effective feedback addresses where to go next. Do not say SBI includes the next step.
facts.reference_hint: Hattie and Timperley (2007), feed up question 'where to next'

facts.statement: Specific goals lead to better performance than vague goals such as 'do your best', which supports making the next step concrete rather than general.
facts.caveat: From goal-setting research, mostly on work tasks the person has accepted and can do. Use only to support concreteness; do not claim that a next step the person helped set is proven to work better.

facts.statement: Feedback is generally best given soon after the event, while both people remember the details and there is a chance to act on it the next time.
facts.caveat: Widely recommended in practice; research on immediate versus delayed feedback is mixed and mostly from learning tasks, so say 'soon', not 'immediately', and avoid claiming a time window. Choose a private, calm moment.

facts.statement: Treating feedback as a two-way conversation, by asking how the other person saw it and listening, gives the giver their view and lets the next step be agreed rather than imposed.
facts.caveat: Strongest support is from education research on feedback as dialogue and from practitioner guidance; it is not a measured guarantee of change at work. Present as good practice.

facts.statement: Specific positive feedback also changes behaviour, because it tells the person exactly what worked so they can keep doing it, which a general 'great job' does not.
facts.caveat: Reasoning follows the same logic as F1 and F3; the clearest research support is that feedback is useful in proportion to the task information it carries. Do not claim that praise always improves performance.

facts.statement: The feedback sandwich, praise then criticism then praise, is popular, but there is little solid evidence that it helps people change behaviour, and it can blur the main message.
facts.caveat: Evidence is thin either way, so do not present it as best practice and do not claim it is proven harmful. If mentioned, say only that the lesson's structure does not depend on it. Not a main topic.

terms.definition: What could be seen or heard, such as 'the meeting ran twenty minutes over', as opposed to a label such as 'disorganised'.
What the behaviour did to the work, the people or the results.
A concrete action the two people agree the person will take next time.

not_claimed: Any percentage for how much of communication is words, tone or body language (the 7-38-55 figure is a misreading of narrow studies)
A fixed ratio of positive to negative comments that guarantees good performance
That the feedback sandwich is proven best practice
That Situation-Behavior-Impact is proven better than other feedback models
That a good conversation, or the person nodding, shows behaviour will change
That people can be matched to feedback by learning style
That feedback must be given immediately, in public, or at a stated number of hours
Any statistic about how many managers or employees give or want feedback
